## Judges 8 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — Ephraim's Complaint
The men of Ephraim confront Gideon fiercely because he did not summon them at the start of the battle against Midian. Ellicott notes Ephraim's historic "arrogance" stemmed from its strength, the memory of Joseph, and the leadership of Joshua; this tribe regularly assumed a right of pre-eminence. Gill adds they "envied the glory" Gideon had gained and feared the tribe of Manasseh would eclipse them. The verb "contended" (Hebrew *riyb*) can mean "to conduct a legal case"; paired with "vigorously" (*chozqah*), the phrase suggests near-violent confrontation — Precept Austin quotes Block: "they accused him fiercely." Enduring Word (Guzik) notes Ephraim "cared more about recognition than the overall good of Israel." Their jealousy surface after, not before, the victory; they had participated (Judges 7:24–25) but wanted the honour of being called first.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_8_commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/

### v. 2 — Gideon's Gentle Reply
Gideon answers with a proverb: "Are not the gleanings of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?" Gill explains: Gideon's own "vintage" (the initial rout) was less than Ephraim's "gleaning" — capturing the two princes Oreb and Zeeb. The Targum renders it, "Are not the weak of the house of Ephraim better than the strong of the house of Abiezer?" Ellicott sees "noble self-control" in Gideon — he waives self-assertion for the sake of national unity, knowing the enemy kings are still at large. Enduring Word says Gideon "soothed their pride by complimenting them" but hints this diplomacy may mask a deeper rivalry that later surfaces in his making of the ephod (v. 27). Precept Austin cites Proverbs 15:1: "a gentle answer turns away wrath."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/

### v. 3 — Their Anger Subsides
Gideon credits God: "God has delivered Oreb and Zeeb into your hand." He again diminishes his own role — "What was I able to do compared to you?" — and their "anger" (*ruach*, literally "wind" or fierce breathing) abates. Ellicott quotes Bishop Hall: "Gideon's good words were as victorious as his sword." Gill notes this "gratified their pride." Precept Austin observes a pattern: after a great victory, internal quarrels often surface among God's people (citing Acts 5–6). The episode shows Gideon at his best — a peacemaker — before the darker tone of the rest of the chapter.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_8_commentary

### v. 4 — Faint Yet Pursuing
Gideon and his 300 cross the Jordan "exhausted yet still in pursuit." Ellicott explains the Hebrew literally says "faint and pursuing," where the "and" is explanatory — exhausted *with* pursuing. Keil (cited in Precept Austin) reads it the same way. Enduring Word quotes Spurgeon: "If a man has never tired himself with working for God, I should think he never has done any work that was worth doing." The verse resumes the narrative of Judges 7:23; the Ephraim episode (vv. 1–3) is inserted parenthetically. This tenacity is one of Gideon's great strengths.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_8_commentary

### v. 5 — Request to Succoth
Gideon asks the men of Succoth for bread. Gill notes Succoth was an Israelite city in the territory of Gad (Joshua 13:27), named after Jacob's booths (Genesis 33:17). Gideon's request is modest — "loaves" (literally "morsels of bread") — and polite ("please"). He explains his troops are faint and he is pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, "kings of Midian." Ellicott observes Gideon did not "requisition" them for fighting, only for bread — an act of common humanity. These were fellow Israelites being asked to support their own deliverers.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm

### vv. 6–7 — Succoth's Refusal and Gideon's Vow
The leaders refuse: "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession?" Ellicott: the phrase is proverbial — "Is the fist of the enemy in your hand?" — implying Gideon hasn't yet won, so helping him is too risky. Gill says they feared Midianite reprisal and "derided him and his small number." Gideon vows: when the LORD delivers the kings, "I will tear your flesh with thorns and briers." Ellicott notes the verb could mean "thresh" — a brutal punishment where victims were dragged over thorns, perhaps even with a threshing sledge. Enduring Word quotes Spurgeon defending Gideon: "when a man is at war, he is not in the habit of sprinkling his adversaries with rosewater." Precept Austin includes Wiersbe's classification of Succoth as "the cynical" — those with no faith in God.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_8_commentary

### vv. 8–9 — Penuel's Refusal and Threatened Tower
At Penuel (also in Gad, east of Jordan), Gideon receives the identical refusal. He threatens: "When I return in triumph, I will tear down this tower!" Ellicott explains Penuel means "face of God" (from Jacob's vision, Genesis 32:30); the tower was their fortified citadel. Their refusal, like Succoth's, was a failure of faith — they waited for victory to be assured before committing. Bridgeway Bible Commentary (via studylight.org) suggests they "feared that if they helped Gideon, the Midianites would later return and punish them." Precept Austin notes Gideon responds in faith ("when," not "if").

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/judges-8.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/

### v. 10 — The Remnant at Karkor
Zebah and Zalmunna are at Karkor with about 15,000 men — all that remain of the eastern armies. One hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had fallen. Gill calculates the original host at 135,000 fighting men (plus non-combatants). Ellicott notes Karkor may mean "a safe enclosure" — the Midianites felt secure, far from the original battlefield. The staggering casualty ratio (120,000 of 135,000 fallen) underscores the supernatural nature of God's deliverance.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm

### v. 11 — A Surprise Attack
Gideon approaches by the caravan route east of Nobah and Jogbehah, taking the Midianites by surprise. Ellicott says he took a wide circuit through nomad territory to avoid the main road — another stratagem to compensate for his small force. The camp "felt secure," not expecting pursuit so far or so fast. Enduring Word suggests Gideon was emboldened because "he saw God do great things in similar circumstances before."

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/

### v. 12 — The Kings Captured
Zebah and Zalmunna flee but Gideon captures them and routs their entire army. Gill notes they were left alone and easily taken once their host scattered. Ellicott connects Psalm 83:13–14 to this flight: "like a wheel… like stubble before the wind." The word "discomfited" (margin: "terrified") suggests a second God-sent panic. The pursuit is complete.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm

### v. 13 — Return by the Ascent of Heres
Gideon returns from battle. Ellicott argues the phrase "before the sun was up" (KJV) is better rendered "from the ascent of Heres" (a place-name, as in LXX and Syriac), not a time reference. The route may have been chosen to approach Succoth from an unexpected direction. Gill and older Jewish commentators (Jarchi, Kimchi) read it as "before sunset," meaning Gideon fought by day and returned the same day.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm

### v. 14 — The Young Man of Succoth
Gideon captures a young man from Succoth and interrogates him. The youth writes down the names of 77 leaders and elders. Ellicott sees the number 77 as significant — perhaps a local council modelled on the 70 elders of Israel (Numbers 11:16) plus seven presiding sheikhs — indicating Succoth was a substantial city. Gill remarks that Gideon showed "great wisdom and strict justice" in identifying the specific culprits rather than punishing indiscriminately.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm

### v. 15 — Confronting Succoth
Gideon presents the captured kings: "Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me." He repeats the leaders' own words verbatim, adding "weary" to heighten their guilt. Gill notes Gideon had "carefully observed and laid up in his memory" their exact taunt. This public vindication precedes the promised punishment.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm

### v. 16 — Disciplining Succoth
Gideon takes the elders and "disciplined" (literally "taught" or "made to know") them with desert thorns and briers. Ellicott says the verb may actually be "threshed" — a horrific punishment where victims were dragged or scourged with thorn-branches. Gill notes the Targum reads "he broke upon them the men of Succoth," and it is unclear whether they died. Precept Austin's Wiersbe calls them "the cynical" who paid dearly for lack of faith. This is one of the episodes that leads commentators like Block (cited by Precept Austin) to say Gideon became "a tyrant, arbitrary in his treatment of the enemy and ruthless in his handling of his own countrymen."

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_8_commentary

### v. 17 — Penuel's Tower Destroyed
Gideon pulls down the tower of Penuel and kills the men of the city. Gill suggests they may have resisted when he came to demolish the tower, or fled into it and were killed when it collapsed. Enduring Word notes the text does not fully explain the severity; it supposes the people of Penuel may have been "significant supporters of the Midianites and traitors against Israel." Precept Austin's Constable describes Gideon as "alarmingly self-assertive and prideful in Judges 8:4–21."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_8_commentary

### v. 18 — The Question at Tabor
Gideon asks the two kings what kind of men they killed at Tabor. They answer: "Men like you — each one resembling the son of a king." Ellicott observes this reveals Gideon had a tall, commanding presence (like Saul later, 1 Samuel 10:24). The mention of Mount Tabor connects to earlier Midianite oppression (Judges 6:2 — Israelites hid in caves there) but the exact battle is otherwise unrecorded. Enduring Word notes Gideon wanted the confession public before exacting blood-vengeance.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/

### v. 19 — "They Were My Brothers"
Gideon reveals the slain men were his own brothers, "the sons of my mother." He swears "as surely as the LORD lives" that if they had spared his brothers, he would spare them. Gill explains this as the law of the blood-avenger (*goel*): the kings were murderers of his kin, not merely enemy combatants, so Gideon had a legal obligation to execute them. Ellicott concurs: Gideon acts as *goel* (Numbers 35:12).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm

### v. 20 — Jether's Fear
Gideon orders his firstborn son Jether to execute the kings — partly to train him in fearlessness, partly to give him prestige, and partly to add to the disgrace of the Midianites (Ellicott). But the youth "was fearful because he was still a youth" and could not draw his sword. Enduring Word suggests Gideon may have remembered his own earlier fears and God's patience with him (Wiersbe, cited in Precept Austin).

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_8_commentary

### v. 21 — Gideon Kills the Kings
The kings ask Gideon to do it himself: "for as the man is, so is his strength" — they prefer a swift death from a warrior to a bungled one from a boy (Ellicott). Gideon kills them and takes the crescent ornaments (*saharonim*, "little moons") from their camels' necks. These were gold or silver lunar-shaped decorations, common among Midianites/Ishmaelites. Ellicott notes even Mohammed found such ornaments on camels after one of his battles.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/

### v. 22 — "Rule Over Us"
The Israelites offer Gideon a hereditary monarchy: "Rule over us — you and your son and grandson." This is the first recorded instance of kingly desires stirring in Israel (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary, via studylight.org). Ellicott notes they saw the advantage of united action under one leader but "forgot that Gideon had received a special call from God." Bridgeway Bible Commentary says they wanted to be "like the nations round about."

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/judges-8.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/judges-8.html

### v. 23 — Gideon Refuses Kingship
Gideon replies: "I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you." This is widely regarded as Gideon's finest moment. Ellicott compares it to George Washington's refusal of a crown, crediting Providence. Enduring Word (Guzik) calls it "the right answer." But Guzik also notes the irony: Gideon's subsequent actions (vv. 24–31) contradict his words — "his words were humble, but his actions were not." Constable (cited in Precept Austin) says "Gideon's subsequent decision belied his words: he led Israel back into idolatry."

**Tradition note — Baptist:** The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary calls this refusal right, noting "Had Gideon been an Ephraimite rather than a Manassite he might have succumbed, but he steadfastly refused."

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_8_commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/judges-8.html

### vv. 24–26 — Gideon Gathers a Fortune
Gideon requests the gold earrings from the plunder (the enemies were Ishmaelites, who wore them). The people gladly give. The total: 1,700 shekels of gold — roughly 40–75 pounds (Cundall, cited in studylight.org) — plus crescent ornaments, pendants, purple royal garments, and camel chains. Enduring Word (Guzik) comments that although the people gave gladly and Gideon arguably deserved reward, "it was inappropriate, because it lifted him far above the level of the people he would lead, and it was at their expense." Guzik adds a practical rule: "Christian leaders who make their living from the gifts of God's people should live at the level of their own people — not below or above."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/judges-8.html

### v. 27 — The Ephod Becomes a Snare
Gideon makes an ephod from the gold and places it in Ophrah. "All Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it there," and it became a "snare" to Gideon and his household.

**What was the ephod?** The ephod was the high priest's sacred vestment (Exodus 28), associated with the Urim and Thummim for inquiring of God. Commentators debate whether Gideon's ephod was:
- A replica of the high-priestly garment (Keil & Delitzsch, cited in studylight.org and Enduring Word)
- A solid gold image or idol (some scholars, per studylight.org)
- A reconstructed Baal shrine (Block, cited in Precept Austin)

**Why did Gideon do it?** Several theories:
- To compete with the tabernacle at Shiloh (in Ephraim's territory), continuing the rivalry from vv. 1–3 (Guzik/Enduring Word)
- Because the high priesthood had lost credibility, and Gideon — who had received direct revelation from God — felt justified in creating a local means of inquiring of the LORD (Keil, cited in studylight.org)
- From good intentions that went awry (Benson's Commentary: Gideon "did this with an honest mind" but fell into "superstition and will-worship")

**Tradition differences:**
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Stresses that the ephod itself "was not an idol but became a snare all the same"; artistic beauty can distract from the LORD. "Gideon handled adversity better than success."
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Says "It does not seem probable that Gideon intended for the thing to become an object of worship… His good intentions were not according to the Lord's will."
- **Reformed/Evangelical (Constable, via studylight.org):** Gideon became "the second official sponsor of idolatry in Israel… Aaron being the first."
- **Older commentators (Benson, Methodist-leaning):** Lists multiple sins: (1) superstition and will-worship, (2) presumption in wearing/causing priests to wear the ephod, which was exclusive to the high priest, (3) transgression of the command to worship at one place (Deuteronomy 12), (4) making a division among the people, (5) laying a stumbling-block.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/judges-8.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/8-27.html
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_8_commentary

### v. 28 — Forty Years of Rest
Midian is subdued and "did not raise its head again." The land rests 40 years "in the days of Gideon." This is the standard formula for a successful judge — the goal of the deliverance cycle is rest. Precept Austin notes this verse is the summary statement the reader expected earlier, delayed by the complications of vv. 1–27.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_8_commentary

### vv. 29–30 — Gideon's Harem and Seventy Sons
"Jerubbaal" (Gideon's other name) settles at home. He has 70 sons from "many wives." Enduring Word (Guzik) observes that a harem reflected not only sexual indulgence but a proud display of wealth: "Look at all the wives and children I can support." Though the Old Testament never directly condemns polygamy, it consistently shows its bitter fruit (Jacob, David, and now Gideon — his son Abimelech will kill 69 of his 70 brothers in Judges 9). Guzik adds: "The Old Testament shows the bitter fruit of polygamy."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/

### v. 31 — Abimelech: "My Father Is King"
Gideon's concubine in Shechem bears him a son whom he names Abimelech — meaning "my father is king." Enduring Word (Guzik) argues this reveals Gideon's true ambition: "It seems that Gideon intended that his son would become the leader of Israel after Gideon himself was gone." Despite verbally refusing kingship (v. 23), Gideon lived and named his children as if he were a king. F.B. Meyer (via studylight.org) comments that "the evil that men do lives after them" — Gideon's lack of self-control in marriage had much to answer for in the tragedy of Judges 9.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/judges-8.html

### v. 32 — Gideon's Death
Gideon dies "at a ripe old age" and is buried in his father Joash's tomb in Ophrah of the Abiezrites. This is a dignified, peaceful end — in contrast to the violence that will immediately follow. Guzik (Enduring Word) summarises: "We could say that Gideon handled adversity better than success. Success, riches, and prominence brought him down." The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics (via biblehub.com) observes the "routine of daily living proved a greater test of his character than the extreme moment of battle."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/judges/8.htm

### vv. 33–35 — Apostasy and Ingratitude
As soon as Gideon dies, Israel turns back to the Baals, specifically making "Baal-berith" (meaning "Baal of the covenant") their god. They forgot the LORD who delivered them and "did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal." Enduring Word (Guzik) notes the tragic irony: by serving Baal, Israel imitated the Gideon of his later years, who valued money and success above God. F.B. Meyer (via studylight.org) calls this "great fickleness and instability" and cites Bunyan's spiritual adversary whispering "I'll cool you, I'll cool you" — a warning about the cooling of devotion. The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics stresses that "the natural mind acts always thus, in the face of the plainest signs of Divine intervention… building itself out from the Unseen by human authorities and institutions."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-8/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/judges-8.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/judges/8.htm

## Summary of Key Themes and Points of Difference Among Traditions

**Areas of broad agreement across traditions:**
- Gideon's handling of Ephraim (vv. 1–3) is a model of wise, peacemaking leadership.
- Gideon's refusal of kingship (v. 23) is doctrinally right: the LORD alone is King.
- The ephod (v. 27) was a catastrophic spiritual failure, whatever Gideon's intentions.
- Gideon's later years show a tragic decline from faith into compromise.

**Where traditions nuanced differently (from available sources):**

| Issue | View |
|---|---|
| **Gideon's violence (vv. 16–17)** | **Spurgeon/Enduring Word** defend it as necessary wartime severity. **Block/Constable (modern evangelical)** see it as evidence of Gideon's moral decline into tyranny. |
| **The ephod's nature (v. 27)** | **Baptist (Garner-Howes)** emphasises good intentions gone wrong. **Reformed/Constable** sees outright idolatry (Gideon as "second Aaron"). **Keil & Delitzsch** see usurpation of the Aaronic priesthood due to Shiloh's corruption. **Benson (Methodist-leaning)** catalogues multiple sins including will-worship and schism. |
| **Gideon's polygamy (v. 30)** | **Enduring Word (Guzik)** treats it as pride and sexual indulgence, noting the OT shows polygamy's bitter fruit without directly condemning it. The NT (Matthew 19:4–6; 1 Timothy 3:2) is understood to supersede this tolerance. |
| **Overall arc** | **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word)** frames it as a warning that success tests character more than adversity. **Evangelical/Reformed** frames it within the Judges cycle of decline. **Baptist (Garner-Howes)** draws five practical lessons about brethren, faith, perseverance, God's rule, and worldly-mindedness. |
